title: The American Experiment
subtitle: From Cane Ridge to the fundamentalist and modernist rupture. How the American church learned to engineer revival, married the market and the flag, and split rather than release the enslaved, and the church that kept the faith through all of it.

sections.title: The Meeting at Cane Ridge
sections.body:
In August 1801, at a Presbyterian meetinghouse on a Kentucky ridge, the American nineteenth century announced itself. The occasion was traditional, a communion season of the kind Scots-Irish Presbyterians had kept for generations, several days of preaching and self-examination gathered around the Lord's table. What happened at Cane Ridge was not traditional. People came from across Kentucky and Ohio by wagon and horse and on foot, camping where they stopped, until contemporary estimates put the crowd at ten to twenty thousand, some said more, in a state whose largest town could not have held a fraction of them. Preaching ran day and night from stands and stumps and wagon beds, Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist preachers working at once within earshot of each other. And the people fell. The host pastor, Barton Stone, later catalogued what he had seen with a taxonomist's care: the falling exercise, the jerks, dancing, laughing, singing that seemed to come from somewhere below the throat. Hundreds lay on the ground at a time, some for hours, rising to profess Christ.

Neither the sneer nor the halo does the event justice. Something real happened at Cane Ridge. Sober witnesses, including skeptical ones, went away shaken; conversions dated from that week held for lifetimes; and the frontier, which the seaboard churches had largely written off as beyond the reach of ordered religion, turned out to be desperate for God. But whatever else Cane Ridge was, it was also the discovery of a form. The camp meeting, the scheduled sacred event that creates its own temporary city, its own crowd, and its own expectations, could be reproduced. The Methodists, characteristically, systematized it within a few years, published manuals on the layout of the grounds, and made the camp meeting an institution of the American West.

The difference from Northampton should be stated exactly, because everything in this essay grows from it. Edwards's awakening had come down on an existing congregation with a settled pastor, a town with a shared discipline, a community that would still be a community in ten years. Cane Ridge assembled strangers, melted them together for a week of intensity no ordinary life could sustain, and dispersed them. The revival was no longer something that happened to a church. The revival was now the church, a church of the event, and its members' deepest religious memory was of a crowd, not a congregation. American Christianity has been trying to get back to that ridge ever since. I say this with a pastor's unease and a historian's confidence: much of what my own tradition calls normal church life, the special meetings, the guest evangelist, the long altar call, is Cane Ridge domesticated and moved indoors.

The awakening that began in such places, the one historians call the Second Great Awakening, ran for a generation and changed the religious composition of the nation. In the settled East it wore a more decorous face, in colleges and town churches. On the frontier it rode with the Methodist circuit riders, young men, often barely trained and barely paid, who covered enormous circuits in all weathers, preaching daily, organizing classes in cabins, dying young at a rate their own conference minutes recorded without sentimentality. Frontier folk joked that on the worst days nothing was out but crows and Methodist preachers. Francis Asbury, their bishop, rode farther across America than almost any man of his generation and slept in more strangers' cabins, and by the middle of the century the Methodists, a rounding error at the Revolution, had become the largest religious body in the United States.

Hold both images, the wild ridge and the disciplined rider: for a while America had the event and the class meeting together, the fire and Wesley's hearth. The riders folded converts into weekly classes exactly as Wesley had designed. The question was whether the system or the spectacle would prove to be the thing Americans actually wanted. The rest of this essay is the answer.

sections.title: Every Man His Own Theologian
sections.body:
The historian Nathan Hatch gave the period its definitive reading in The Democratization of American Christianity, and his thesis is simple to state and hard to exhaust: in the half-century after the Revolution, American Christianity was remade from below. The same populist energy that had thrown off a king turned on every other inherited authority, including the learned clergy, the confessions, and the idea that theology required training. Insurgent movements, the Methodists, the Baptists, the Christian and Disciples movements of Barton Stone and Alexander Campbell, the Black churches organizing under their own preachers, grew explosively by trusting ordinary people: preachers who talked like their hearers, hymns set to familiar tunes, cheap tracts and religious newspapers by the ton, and the standing invitation to read the Bible for yourself and judge every doctor of divinity by it. Stone and his colleagues dissolved their own presbytery in 1804 with a document styled as its last will and testament, bequeathing their authority to the people and to Scripture. The slogan of the restorationists said it all: no creed but the Bible.

Say what deserves honor first. The democratizers took the priesthood of all believers more seriously than the Reformers who coined it ever dared. They carried the gospel to people the respectable churches had abandoned, dignified the unlettered convert, and built, in the Methodist classes and Baptist congregations of the backcountry, real communities of discipline and mercy. If Christianity is true, it is true for the tanner and the field hand, and they are competent to receive it. That conviction is biblical, and the movements that acted on it reaped what the seaboard establishments, waiting for the frontier to come to them properly dressed, did not.

But watch what else was being established, because it has never been disestablished since. When every man is his own theologian, the self becomes the seat of religious authority, and eighteen centuries of creed, council, and communion become, at best, advisory. The movements that began by rejecting human tradition in favor of the Bible alone discovered, within a generation, that the Bible alone, read alone, yields as many Christianities as there are readers. The burned-over district of upstate New York, scorched by revival after revival, became the seedbed of entirely new religions: Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon in 1830 a few counties from where William Miller's followers, having calculated the Second Coming for 1844, sold their farms and waited. The free market of faith produced what free markets produce, innovation without limit and no mechanism but popularity for telling bread from stone.

And the market itself must be named plainly, because this is the rehearsal for everything this platform means when it says consumer religion. With no established church, every congregation in America competed for adherents against every other, and the adherent, for the first time in Christian history at national scale, was a chooser. Denominations multiplied and subdivided; a town of a thousand souls might hold five competing churches, each needing to be chosen to survive. Alexis de Tocqueville, touring in the 1830s, marveled that disestablished religion in America seemed stronger, not weaker, than Europe's state churches, so woven into mores that he judged it the first of the republic's political institutions. He was right about the strength. What he could not yet see was the price of acquiring strength this particular way: a church that lives by being chosen will, under pressure, become the kind of thing people choose, and the line between evangelism and salesmanship, already thin in Whitefield's day, was about to be erased on principle.

I write from deep inside this inheritance, not above it. The Baptist church I pastor is congregational, revivalist, and voluntary to the bone; nobody is in the room on Sunday who did not choose to be. I believe in that. Uncoerced faith is honest faith, and the democratizers were right that God is no respecter of diplomas. I have also watched what the sovereignty of the religious consumer does to a congregation's soul, mine included; the nineteenth century is where we learned it. The individualist lens, the assumption that my judgment, my experience, and my preferences are the final court of religious appeal, was not smuggled into American Christianity by the culture. We built it in, on purpose, and called it freedom. It was partly that. The next figure in the story shows what it became.

sections.title: The Machinery of Revival
sections.body:
Charles Grandison Finney was a young lawyer in upstate New York when he was converted, dramatically and alone, in the woods and the law office, in October 1821. His Memoirs record that when a client's case was called the next morning, he answered that he held a retainer from the Lord Jesus Christ to plead his cause and could not plead the client's. The sentence is perfect Finney: the courtroom, the contract, the immediate total reassignment of his talents. He took the bar's methods with him into the pulpit, examining his hearers like a prosecutor, addressing them as "you," singular, and pressing for a verdict on the spot, because a lawyer does not send the jury home to think it over.

Through the late 1820s and the 1830s Finney became the most consequential revivalist in America, and his Rochester campaign in the winter of 1830 and 1831 became the pattern: months of coordinated meetings across cooperating churches, the town's business class converted in numbers, contemporaries reporting taverns closing and a changed city. With the fame came the fight. His so-called new measures scandalized the established revival men: protracted meetings night after night, prayer for sinners by name from the pulpit, women praying aloud in mixed assemblies, and above all the anxious bench, a seat at the front to which the almost-persuaded were summoned publicly, there to be prayed over and pressed to decide. Older evangelicals, led by Lyman Beecher and Asahel Nettleton, met Finney at New Lebanon in 1827 to rein him in. They failed, and their failure was a fork in the road for a whole civilization's religion.

In 1835 Finney published Lectures on Revivals of Religion, and in its opening lecture he set down the sentence, or nearly, on which everything after him stands. A revival of religion, he argued there, is not a miracle, but the result of the right use of the appropriate means, as truly as a crop of wheat results from the right use of plow and seed. The wording I have given is his argument stated nearly in his words; the claim itself is not in dispute, because he built the whole book on it. God has established means; the means, rightly worked, produce the effect; a church without revival is a farmer who did not plant. Edwards had titled his report A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God. Finney wrote a manual so that no one need ever be surprised again.

Be fair to the man before weighing the machine, because Finney was no cynic. He preached the holiness of God and the horror of sin with an urgency his critics rarely matched; he demanded that converts prove conversion in reformed lives; and his moral seriousness ran straight into the great cause: Finney made opposition to slavery a test of fellowship at his meetings, and Oberlin, the Ohio college he served as professor and then president, admitted Black students and women when almost no American college would, and became a depot of the Underground Railroad. Set beside the respectable churches that kept slaveholders on their rolls and theology journals that debated the question at leisure, Finney's record shames most of his critics. If pragmatism about means had always been welded, as it was in him, to conscience about ends, this section would read differently.

But the weld did not hold, because it could not be inherited. What could be inherited was the method, and the method carried a theology inside it whether its users ever opened the Lectures or not. If revival is the result of means, then the measure of ministry is measurable response; if conversion can be produced, it can be counted, forecast, and improved; and the awful possibility Edwards spent Religious Affections guarding against, that a stirred crowd and a saving work might be two different things, becomes not a warning but an inefficiency. The anxious bench in time became the altar call, the altar call became the raised hand with every head bowed, and the numbers became the report card of the American pastor. I am not describing other people. I am a revivalist Baptist by blood; I was raised counting decisions, and I have stood at the front and counted them myself, and I know the particular temptation to preach for the response the count requires. Finney did not invent that temptation. He baptized it, wrote its handbook, and called it the right use of means. We have been using the means ever since, mostly without his conscience and always without his excuse.

sections.title: When We Chose Slavery
sections.body:
Now the section I would rather not write, which is why it must sit at the center of this essay. I am a Baptist pastor. What follows is not the story of what some churches did somewhere. It is the story of what my church did, and when I write we, I mean it without a millimeter of distance.

It did not have to go the way it went, and for a moment it looked as if it might not. In the glow after the Revolution, with liberty in every mouth, the evangelical movements flirted seriously with their own logic. The Methodists wrote rules against slaveholding into their founding American discipline in 1784 and abandoned enforcing them within months under southern pressure. Virginia Baptists heard emancipationist voices in the 1780s and let them fall silent. Then the cotton gin came in 1793, the interior opened, and slavery, which some founders had consoled themselves was dying, became the most profitable system on the continent. The churches grew with the country, southern wealth grew with cotton, and the price of saying what Methodists had said in 1784 went up every year until nobody with a building and a budget would pay it.

What the churches did instead of repenting was exegete. A formidable biblical defense of slavery was assembled, and it was not stupid, which is the terrifying part. Abraham held slaves; the Mosaic law regulated rather than abolished the institution; Paul returned Onesimus and told slaves to obey their masters; nowhere does the New Testament command emancipation. Southern divines argued from the plain sense of the text, the same plain sense the democratized church had made its only authority, and they were better proof-texters than most of their opponents. Against them stood the deeper argument: one blood in Adam, the image of God, a gospel in which "there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28), and the whole trajectory of Scripture bending against the auction block, which in its American form, race-based, hereditary, married to kidnapping and the deliberate breaking of families, matched nothing in Moses anyway. The argument that was easier to make from isolated verses was wrong. The nation's Bible-reading method could not prove it wrong. Hold that thought for Lincoln.

In 1844 and 1845 the two largest evangelical bodies in America tore in half, and the occasions could not have been more precise. The Methodist General Conference of 1844 found that one of its bishops, James O. Andrew of Georgia, had come to own slaves, and asked him to desist from exercising his office while he did; the southern conferences refused the rebuke and organized the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, in 1845. The Baptists made it a test case on purpose. Georgia Baptists proposed a slaveholder, James Reeve, for appointment as a missionary, expressly noting what he was; Alabama Baptists demanded a ruling that slaveholders were eligible for all appointments; and the mission board in Boston answered that it could never be a party to an arrangement that would imply approval of slavery. So in May 1845, in Augusta, Georgia, the southern churches founded a new body to send out missionaries without that impediment. That body is the Southern Baptist Convention. My convention, the largest Protestant denomination in America, was organized so that a man could hold human beings in bondage and carry the gospel at the same time, and the founders saw no contradiction, and they were our founders. The Presbyterians, already strained in 1837, completed their own division when the war came.

Frederick Douglass, who had lived under the lash of praying masters, wrote in the appendix to his 1845 Narrative that between the Christianity of this land and the Christianity of Christ he recognized the widest possible difference. He was not being rhetorical. He was being exact, and the churches he indicted answered him with sermons on the curse of Ham.

It took my people a hundred and fifty years to say plainly what Douglass said in 1845. In June 1995, meeting in Atlanta on its hundred-fiftieth anniversary, the Southern Baptist Convention passed a resolution on racial reconciliation that named the truth at last: that the convention's founding was bound up with the defense of slavery, that Southern Baptists had defended segregation and white supremacy in the generations after, that this was sin against God and against Black brothers and sisters, and that we repent and ask forgiveness. I am glad we said it. I refuse to be proud that it took us until 1995. A century and a half is not a long time for God. It was a very long time for the people who waited, and some of what they built while they waited is the next section, and it is the most Christian thing in this whole American story.

sections.title: The Faith They Kept
sections.body:
Richard Allen was born enslaved in 1760, converted under Methodist preaching as a young man, and did something that still stops me every time I trace it: he took the religion practiced by the people who owned him, looked past them, and recognized the God who was against them. He preached to his own master with such effect that the man became convinced slaveholding was sin and let Allen contract for his own freedom, which he earned with years of extra labor. By the 1780s he was a free man and a licensed Methodist preacher in Philadelphia, rising at five in the morning to preach the early services at St. George's church, where the Black membership grew under his ministry until the white membership decided it had grown too large.

In Allen's own telling, the break came during prayer, around 1787: he and Absalom Jones and other Black members, kneeling in a gallery they had been moved to, were pulled up from their knees by white trustees who told them they were in the wrong seats and could finish praying afterward. They finished the prayer. Then they walked out together, and, as Allen remembered it, the church lost its Black members in a body. What they built next they built twice, because they would not build in bitterness: first the Free African Society, a mutual aid society for the free Black community, and then congregations. When yellow fever devastated Philadelphia in 1793 and much of the white establishment fled the city, Allen and Jones organized Black Philadelphians to nurse the sick and bury the dead, served through the whole horror, were accused afterward in print of profiteering, and published a documented reply.

Jones went on to become the first Black priest of the Episcopal Church. Allen stayed Methodist, because he judged, in his plain words as he recalled them, that no religious sect suited the capacity of plain people as well. His congregation, Bethel, was dedicated in 1794 by Bishop Asbury himself, and then Allen spent twenty years in legal trench warfare with white Methodist elders who claimed authority over the property and the pulpit, until the Pennsylvania Supreme Court settled Bethel's independence in early 1816. That April, Black Methodist congregations from several cities met in Philadelphia and organized the African Methodist Episcopal Church, the first fully independent Black denomination in the United States, and consecrated Allen its first bishop. Mark the sequence: they did not leave over doctrine, and they did not leave the faith. They kept Wesley's doctrine, Wesley's discipline, and Wesley's hymns, and left the people who would not let them pray. It is the cleanest separation of Christianity from its abusers in American history.

In the South, where independent Black churches were feared as insurrection in embryo, the faith went underground instead. After a planned rising was attributed to Denmark Vesey in Charleston in 1822, that city's AME congregation, one of the largest in the country, was suppressed and its building destroyed; after Nat Turner, a slave preacher, led the bloody Southampton revolt in 1831, states across the South tightened laws against teaching enslaved people to read and against Black preaching without white supervision. So the enslaved church met where it could not be watched, in the woods and swamps and cabins, in brush arbors and hush harbors, praying into overturned pots to swallow the sound, and historians have long called it the invisible institution. Its members heard the whole Bible, including every chapter their masters needed them not to hear. The masters knew it: an abridged Scripture printed in London in 1807 for missionary use among the enslaved of the British Caribbean cut the Bible down for safety, and the escape from Egypt did not survive the cut. The praying church in the woods put Exodus back, and set it to music. The spirituals are that church's theology, Go Down Moses, the sweet chariot, Daniel delivered and why not every man, a body of song in which lament and hope are fused at a depth the white church's hymnals of the same years, and I have shelves of them, almost never reach. When the enslaved sang about crossing Jordan, they meant heaven, and the Ohio River, and both meanings were faith.

Every honest history of American Christianity turns on this fact. The people to whom the gospel was brought shackled to the worst thing America ever built took the gospel and judged the shackles with it. They read the Book their masters handed them more truly than the masters did. The church my tradition betrayed for cotton was kept, whole and praying and singing, by the people the betrayal crushed, and the prophet's cry they sang was Scripture's own: "But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream" (Amos 5:24). If God preserved a faithful witness in nineteenth-century America, this is where it worshiped. Any account of this century that treats the Black church as a subplot has confused the plot with the publicity.

sections.title: The Almighty Has His Own Purposes
sections.body:
The war, when it came, was the most religious war in American history, and that is an indictment of everyone concerned. Both armies were full of praying men; revivals swept the camps, especially the Confederate camps in the winters of 1863 and 1864, and tens of thousands of soldiers professed conversion between battles. Both nations claimed the Christian God by name. The Confederacy wrote an invocation of Almighty God into its constitution, and its preachers assured the South that it was Israel, set apart and afflicted. The North sang Julia Ward Howe's Battle Hymn of the Republic, published in 1862, which read the Union army as the instrument of the coming of the Lord, Christ's sacrifice and the soldier's fused in a single verse. Sermons north and south blessed the cannon with equal confidence and the same concordance. The political lens, the habit of reading one's own nation, party, and army as God's cause, is not a modern corruption of a purer American faith. It marched in both directions at once in 1861, fully formed, out of the pulpits.

Mark Noll has argued, and this essay follows him, that the Civil War was a theological crisis and not only a political one. The democratized American church had staked everything on one method: the plain sense of the Bible, available to every honest reader. On slavery, the method deadlocked. The proof-texts, read plainly, served the slaveholder; the deeper argument from creation and gospel required exactly the kind of interpretive reach the populist churches had taught two generations to distrust. The preachers could not settle it, so the generals did. A civilization that had made the Bible its only common authority learned that it possessed no agreed way to read it, and the learning cost three-quarters of a million lives.

Into that wreckage, on 4 March 1865, with the war nearly won and every incentive to preach the triumph of God's cause, Abraham Lincoln delivered a second inaugural address of barely seven hundred words, and it remains the most searching public theology any American has ever spoken. He observed that both sides read the same Bible and prayed to the same God, each invoking His aid against the other, and he declined to be surprised that neither side's prayers had been answered in full. Then he said the sentence the pulpits of neither section had found the honesty to say: "The Almighty has His own purposes." He went further. He proposed that American slavery might be an offense God now willed to remove, and the war itself the woe due to those by whom the offense came, due, he was careful to say, to North and South together, the whole nation that had profited by the bondsman's two hundred and fifty years of unrequited toil. And he ended not in vindication but in charity, with malice toward none, binding up wounds. The president, a man of no church, melancholy and scripture-soaked, read providence against his own side's applause, judged both nations under God, and asked for mercy on everyone. No cause but God's own came out of that speech intact.

It stings a pastor to write the obvious sentence, so I will write it slowly. The deepest American sermon of the nineteenth century was not preached by any of us. The trained clergy of two nations, holding the largest Bible-reading audience on earth, spent four years assuring their congregations that God was a partisan, and the theological correction came from a politician on a platform, quoting the Psalms over the graves both sides had filled. When this platform says the political lens is old, this is what it means. We did not acquire the habit of conscripting God in some later, coarser generation. We had already perfected it by 1865, and the man who called us on it was outside the guild.

The war ended; the habit did not. The South, having lost, built a civil religion around its loss, the Lost Cause, in which the Confederate dead became martyrs and the old order was draped in stained glass, and white Protestant churches were its custodians. The North, having won, took the victory as heaven's verdict on the Union and its expanding commerce, which proved an equally durable theology and a more profitable one. Two errors, one instrument. Fifty years later their grandchildren would wave flags in the same sanctuaries for a world war, and a century later for culture wars, and the sermons would change little. Lincoln's sentence has been available the whole time.

sections.title: Souls by the Numbers
sections.body:
Dwight L. Moody sold shoes. That is not a jibe; it is the key to the man and the era. Fatherless from the age of four, barely schooled, he was a Boston shoe clerk of eighteen when his Sunday school teacher, Edward Kimball, walked into the stockroom in 1855 and spoke to him about Christ, and he was converted among the boots. He moved to Chicago, sold more shoes, and applied a salesman's energy to the Lord's work: a mission Sunday school in the slums that swelled into the hundreds, leadership of the city's YMCA, tireless personal work. He was never ordained. After the great fire of 1871 burned his church, his house, and his city, Moody gave himself wholly to evangelism, and in 1873 he sailed for Britain an unknown and came back, after two years of enormous campaigns in Edinburgh, Glasgow, and London, the most famous preacher in the English-speaking world.

What Moody built for his American campaigns in the 1870s and 1880s belongs in the vocabulary of the corporation. Before he came to a city, there was an executive committee of pastors and, crucially, businessmen; a guarantee fund raised in advance; a rented or purpose-built hall seating thousands; a trained choir of hundreds under Ira Sankey, whose gospel songs, sentimental, memorable, pitched at the heart, were half the draw; corps of ushers; saturation publicity in the newspapers, which Moody courted as skillfully as any man of his age; and the inquiry room, where trained workers received those moved by the sermon and recorded the results. The businessmen were not incidental. Chicago merchants and manufacturers like Cyrus McCormick backed him; in Philadelphia, the merchant John Wanamaker turned a former railroad freight depot over to Moody's campaign in the winter of 1875 and 1876, and when the revival closed, Wanamaker opened his department store in the same building. Souls in winter, dry goods in spring, one address. I do not know a cleaner image for this whole century, and none of the participants saw anything to blush at, which is the point.

The man himself was better than the machine he normalized. Moody preached a warm, simple gospel of God's love with tears on his face; he liked to say, in words his hearers remembered and repeated, that he looked on this world as a wrecked vessel and God had given him a lifeboat and said to save all he could. He refused to grow rich, gave his book royalties away, founded schools for poor students, and in 1886 founded the Chicago training institute, renamed for him after his death, to raise up what he called men to stand in the gap, lay workers for the cities' unreached. His kindness was famous, his ego by celebrity standards small. If the revival-as-production had a saint, it was Moody.

But watch what has happened between Cane Ridge and Moody, because it happened almost silently, under cover of good intentions. Revival, which Edwards called a surprising work of God, and which Finney recast as the right use of means, is now an urban production with a budget, a venue, a marketing plan, a musical program, and a results department. The crowd is gathered by the same instruments that gather a crowd for anything, because that is what instruments are; the response is tallied like inventory, because a guarantee fund requires a report. And the gospel, preached sincerely by a sincere man, is now packaged, a product optimized for the widest possible reception, its songs chosen for reach, its sermons timed for effect.

The generation after Moody dropped the modesty and kept the production. Billy Sunday, a former major-league outfielder converted at a Chicago mission, took the platform with an athlete's body and a vaudevillian's timing, sliding across the stage as if into home plate, smashing chairs, damning demon rum in slang the papers printed gleefully, while his organization ran campaigns through purpose-built wooden tabernacles floored with sawdust, down whose aisles the convicted came in such numbers that hitting the sawdust trail entered the language. In the Great War his platform fused revival, patriotism, and bond sales into a single roaring act. The distance from the anxious bench to the sawdust trail to the stadium crusade to the arena stage with the countdown clock is short, and my own tradition walked every step of it applauding. Entertainment did not sneak into American church life. We booked it, built the hall for it, and counted the house.

sections.title: The Man Nobody Knows
sections.body:
The new century opened with the Protestant house dividing over a real question, and both parties deserve their strongest voice before either is judged.

Hear the social gospel first, from its best man. Walter Rauschenbusch was a Baptist, one of ours, pastor from 1886 to 1897 of a small German congregation on the edge of Hell's Kitchen in New York, and what radicalized him was not a seminar but a decade of funerals for children who had died of conditions their neighborhood guaranteed. Christianity and the Social Crisis, published in 1907, found an enormous readership, and its case at full strength is simply this: the prophets and Jesus did not address souls floating free of circumstance; they proclaimed the kingdom of God, and they confronted sin not only in hearts but in structures, in courts that sold the needy for a pair of sandals. A Christianity that can see a saloonkeeper's sin but not a landlord's has not risen above its society; it has gone into business with it. Whoever cannot sign at least that much has not argued with Rauschenbusch; he has dodged him. And the man himself prayed, personally and evangelically, to the end; his little book of prayers for the social awakening gives him away.

Now the grief, for it is grief and not scorn. In Rauschenbusch's heirs, more than in him, the kingdom quietly became the progress of civilization, sin became ignorance, the cross became an example rather than an atonement, and the resurrection became negotiable. H. Richard Niebuhr pronounced the verdict on the finished product in one merciless sentence, in The Kingdom of God in America: a God without wrath bringing men without sin into a kingdom without judgment through the ministrations of a Christ without a cross. A message like that asks nothing, forgives nothing, and raises no one from the dead, and the First World War broke the doctrine of progress it rested on.

The conservative answer began seriously. Between 1910 and 1915 twelve paperback volumes called The Fundamentals, ninety essays, many by scholars of real standing, were mailed free to English-speaking pastors and missionaries around the world, some three million copies by the count George Marsden reports, the project funded by two California oil men, Lyman and Milton Stewart. The defense of the faith once delivered was distributed by mass marketing and underwritten by an oil fortune, and no one involved found it strange, because by 1910 no American Christian of any party would have. In 1920 a Baptist editor, Curtis Lee Laws, coined a name for those ready to do battle for the fundamentals, and the movement had its label.

The ablest mind on that side, J. Gresham Machen of Princeton, must be named fairly because almost no one at the time did. His Christianity and Liberalism, in 1923, argued without rancor that liberal theology was not a looser Christianity but a different religion, built on religious feeling rather than on things that happened, and that honesty required saying so; even Walter Lippmann, no believer, commended the book as the strongest statement of its case. Machen's own communion did not refute him. It tried him, suspended him from its ministry in the thirties for refusing to fund a mission board he judged unfaithful, and he died on New Year's Day 1937, founder of a seminary and a small new church, having lost by every visible measure to people who had answered his argument with procedure.

By then the public verdict had come down anyway, in July 1925, in Dayton, Tennessee, where a schoolteacher named John Scopes was tried for teaching evolution. William Jennings Bryan, three times the Democratic nominee for president, a lifelong progressive who feared Darwinism chiefly for the social ruthlessness being drawn from it, and not without cause, since the very textbook at issue taught eugenics without blushing, took the stand for the prosecution and was examined on the Bible by Clarence Darrow while H. L. Mencken filed dispatches of gorgeous contempt. Scopes was convicted and fined a hundred dollars, later overturned on a technicality; Bryan died five days after the trial ended. The fundamentalists won the case and, in the press and the universities and the mind of the American establishment, lost everything else, and Marsden's histories trace the long retreat that followed, into a subculture of separate schools, boards, and radio hours. One party kept the culture and lost the confession. The other kept the confession and left the culture. Neither asked whose categories both were thinking in, and the answer had been on the bestseller lists for months.

In the very year of the Scopes trial, an advertising executive named Bruce Barton, a founder of the agency whose initials still carry his name, published The Man Nobody Knows, and America made it one of the best-selling books in the country through 1926. Barton had grown up on a meek stained-glass Jesus and corrected it with the only categories his industry knew. His Jesus was a magnetic executive and welcome dinner companion who took twelve ordinary men from the bottom ranks and forged the organization that conquered the world; his parables were, Barton argued, the finest advertisements ever written; his ministry, in Barton's telling, made him the founder of modern business. The book is not a parody. It is a mirror, reflecting a Protestantism so thoroughly married to the market that the market could return the compliment and remake Christ in its own image, to general applause, while the theologians were busy in Dayton. Jesus had already ruled on the exchange: "No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money" (Matthew 6:24). Barton quoted other verses.

Close the ledger now, and read it as ours, because it is. We learned at Cane Ridge that the event could be the church; from the democratizers that the self could be the authority; from Finney that conversion could be engineered and counted; from the war that God could be conscripted by both sides at once; from Moody's committees that revival could be capitalized; from Sunday that it could be staged; from Barton that Christ himself could be branded. Consumer, individualist, entertainment, political: every lens this platform spends itself diagnosing was ground and fitted here, mostly by people who loved God and meant well, which is the most frightening sentence in this essay. Underneath the whole story the two witnesses still stand: the Black church, which kept the faith through the worst we did, and Lincoln's sentence, which reads providence better than our sermons do. "The Almighty has His own purposes." We had ours. The American experiment in Christianity is the record of how hard it became to tell the difference, and the record has not closed, because we are still inside it, you and I, reading it through the lenses it made. Wesley's road, awakening bound to formation, ran through this century too, quiet, unprofitable, mostly untaken. It is still open. That is not a comfort. It is a summons.

keyFigures.name: Charles Grandison Finney
keyFigures.note: Lawyer turned revivalist whose Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1835) taught America that revival results from the right use of means.

keyFigures.name: Richard Allen
keyFigures.note: Born enslaved; founded the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816, the first fully independent Black denomination in the United States.

keyFigures.name: Abraham Lincoln
keyFigures.note: His Second Inaugural (1865) read providence against both warring churches: "The Almighty has His own purposes."

keyFigures.name: Dwight L. Moody
keyFigures.note: Shoe salesman turned evangelist who organized mass revival with the methods of the modern corporation.

keyFigures.name: Walter Rauschenbusch
keyFigures.note: Baptist pastor in Hell's Kitchen whose Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907) argued that sin lives in structures as well as hearts.

keyFigures.name: J. Gresham Machen
keyFigures.note: Princeton scholar whose Christianity and Liberalism (1923) argued that liberal theology was a different religion, and who was put out of his church's ministry for acting on it.

keyFigures.name: Bruce Barton
keyFigures.note: Advertising executive whose bestseller The Man Nobody Knows (1925) sold Jesus as the founder of modern business.
